questions.prompt: Manel says: "I met my fiancé through cyberspace." A friend reports it the next day. Which version is right?

options.text: Manel said that she met her fiancé through cyberspace.
Manel said that she has met her fiancé through cyberspace.
Manel said that she had met her fiancé through cyberspace.
Manel said she will meet her fiancé through cyberspace.

questions.explanation: The reporting verb said is in the past, so the reported verb steps one notch further back: a past simple becomes a past perfect, which gives had met, and the pronouns move from I and my to she and her. Keeping the past simple leaves the two events on the same level and loses the step the rule exists to make. A present perfect goes the wrong way, since it is nearer the present than the past simple it is supposed to be reporting. And a future reverses the meaning altogether, turning something that has already happened into something still to come.

questions.prompt: According to the recording of Lesson 26, what proportion of the brain's capacity do we use today?
questions.explanation: The recording says we still make use of only about 20 % of the brain's capacity, and it is from that figure that the speaker builds the rest of his prediction about a larger forehead. 23 % is the number your book prints in a true-or-false exercise precisely so that you have to listen rather than guess, and it is false. 50 % would leave the argument with nowhere to grow towards, and 10 % belongs to a popular saying about the brain that this passage does not use.

questions.prompt: Complete this sentence about a road: "Since the new factory opened, the air has become ……… ."

options.text: more polluted and more polluted than

questions.explanation: One thing is changing steadily in one direction, and polluted is a long adjective, so the structure is more and more followed by the adjective. The double the belongs to the other structure, the one that ties two changes to each other, and this sentence has only one change to describe. Repeating the whole adjective and then adding than turns it into an ordinary comparison, which needs a second term the sentence never supplies. And polluted cannot take -er at all: only short adjectives do, which is why English gives long ones more and more instead.

questions.prompt: Which of these four readers of Lesson 25 writes against excessive internet use?

options.text: Sam, who compares the internet with watching television
Ian, whose wife spends five hours online every evening
Janet, who talks about irrational prejudices
Manel, who met her fiancé online

questions.explanation: Ian is the one clear opponent: he can live without the internet, his wife cannot, and he says plainly that their marriage is suffering as a result. Sam argues the other way, holding that surfing is healthier than sitting in front of a television with no interactivity at all. Janet also argues for it, and her whole point is that judging online conversation more harshly than telephone conversation is an irrational prejudice. And Manel is the message that will not be sorted, since she recounts what her own excessive use cost her and defends the need behind it in the same breath.

questions.prompt: Say these words aloud and find the one whose stress falls on the FIRST syllable.
questions.explanation: newspaper is stressed on NEWS, its first syllable, as compound nouns of this kind usually are. The other three all end in a suffix that pulls the stress towards it: education and addiction end in -tion, which puts the stress on the syllable immediately before, giving eduCAtion and adDICtion, and availability ends in -ity, which does the same and lands on availaBILity, its fourth. That single pattern — the syllable just before -tion, -sion, -ic and -ity — settles most of the words in this exercise without any memorising.
